--- title: "Communicating uncertainty" description: "An interval for the average and an interval for a new catch answer different questions. On the survey the first held few of the catches at new sites and the second nine in ten; conformal prediction gives any model an interval from held-out errors, which holds only at stations like the ones that set it." order: 4 categories: [uncertainty, interpretation] --- ## A prediction is reported with an interval A prediction is one number, and an **interval** says how far from it the truth may lie. Two intervals come from the same model and look alike on a plot, but they answer different questions: - A **confidence interval** says where the **average** lies: the mean outcome over all the places that share a set of inputs, say all water at 8 °C and 100 m. It narrows as more data are collected. - A **prediction interval** says where **one new** observation may land. It adds the scatter of single observations around their average, so it stays wide however much data there is. A question about habitat, such as where the species is most abundant, needs the first. A question about a haul, such as how many animals the next one will bring, needs the second. A prediction interval is checked by its **coverage**, the share of new observations that fall inside it: a 90% interval should hold 9 catches in 10 at sites the model never saw. [Uncertainty and stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) gave a model's score an interval; this page gives its predictions one. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Conformal prediction sets an interval from held-out errors A model fitted with a distribution, such as a GAM with the negative binomial, gives a prediction interval from it. A random forest has no distribution. **Conformal prediction** gives an interval to any model. The sites are split three ways: one part to fit the model, a **calibration** part to measure its errors, and a test part to check the result. Each interval then reaches as far either side of its prediction as 90% of the calibration errors, a little further to allow for the number of calibration sites. Its promise is plain: if new stations are drawn the same way as the calibration ones, 9 in 10 of their catches fall inside. It assumes nothing about the model or the shape of its errors. It also says nothing about stations unlike the calibration ones. ::: {.diagram} ![Three intervals from one model. An interval for the average is narrow and holds few single catches. An interval for a new catch is wide and holds most of them. Conformal prediction sets the width from the errors on calibration sites, so that 9 in 10 catches fall inside at stations like them.](img/three-intervals.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. For the average, a confidence interval: a narrow blue band along a rising line, with grey points for single catches scattered well above and below it; it narrows with more stations. For a new catch, a prediction interval: a wide pale orange band around the same line, holding nearly all the points; it stays wide however many stations. From held-out errors, conformal prediction: a row of bars for the errors on calibration sites, sorted by size, with a dashed line marking where 90% of them end, and an arrow from that line to an interval drawn around a prediction; it holds 9 in 10 at stations like the calibration sites. A note says a prediction interval is checked by its coverage, the share of new catches that fall inside it."} ::: ## Worked example The survey's sites are split three ways: half to fit, a quarter to calibrate and a quarter to test. The GAM of [Black boxes and interpretable models](black-box-or-not.qmd) gives both an interval for the average and one for a new catch. The random forest of [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd) is then given a conformal interval, and is calibrated a second time on stations with little chlorophyll, to see what happens where it is used beyond them. Every interval is a 90% interval, as on that page. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() # whole sites: half to fit, a quarter to calibrate, a quarter to test three_parts <- function(data) { first <- group_initial_split(data, group = site_id, prop = 0.5) second <- group_initial_split(testing(first), group = site_id, prop = 0.5) list(fitting = training(first), calibration = training(second), test = testing(second)) } parts <- three_parts(survey) fitting <- parts$fitting calibration <- parts$calibration test <- parts$test count_recipe <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = fitting ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") map(parts, \(part) tibble(sites = n_distinct(part$site_id), stations = nrow(part))) |> list_rbind(names_to = "part") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|part | sites| stations| |:-----------|-----:|--------:| |fitting | 82| 399| |calibration | 40| 203| |test | 38| 198|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import (HistGradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor) from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, SplineTransformer from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() def halves(frame): grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.5, random_state=123) first, second = next(grouper.split(frame, groups=frame["site_id"])) return frame.iloc[first], frame.iloc[second] # whole sites: half to fit, a quarter to calibrate, a quarter to test def three_parts(frame): fitting, rest = halves(frame) calibration, test = halves(rest) return {"fitting": fitting, "calibration": calibration, "test": test} parts = three_parts(survey) fitting, calibration, test = parts.values() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) def pipeline(model): return Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", model)]) pd.DataFrame([{"part": name, "sites": part["site_id"].nunique(), "stations": len(part)} for name, part in parts.items()]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | part | sites | stations | |:------------|--------:|-----------:| | fitting | 80 | 377 | | calibration | 40 | 199 | | test | 40 | 224 | ::: ::: ::: ### The interval for the average holds few catches The GAM is fitted to the fitting sites. The interval for the average comes from how closely the data pin its curves down, on the log scale, turned back into animals. The interval for a new catch adds the scatter of single catches: the 5% and 95% points of the negative binomial around each expected count. Both are checked on the test sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gam_fit <- workflow(count_recipe) |> add_model( gen_additive_mod() |> set_engine("mgcv", family = mgcv::nb(), method = "REML") |> set_mode("regression"), formula = abundance ~ s(depth_m) + s(temperature_c) + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season ) |> fit(fitting) gam_engine <- extract_fit_engine(gam_fit) baked <- bake(extract_recipe(gam_fit), test) # the expected count on the log scale, and how closely it is known link <- predict(gam_engine, baked, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE) z <- qnorm(0.95) # 1.64 for a 90% interval expected <- exp(link$fit) size <- gam_engine$family$getTheta(TRUE) # the negative binomial's spread gam_intervals <- bind_rows( "For the average" = tibble(low = exp(link$fit - z * link$se.fit), high = exp(link$fit + z * link$se.fit)), "For a new catch" = tibble(low = qnbinom(0.05, mu = expected, size = size), high = qnbinom(0.95, mu = expected, size = size)), .id = "interval" ) |> mutate(predicted = rep(expected, 2), caught = rep(test$abundance, 2), inside = caught >= low & caught <= high) gam_intervals |> summarise(coverage = mean(inside), width = mean(high - low), .by = interval) |> mutate(across(c(coverage, width), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|interval | coverage| width| |:---------------|--------:|-----:| |For the average | 0.20| 2.54| |For a new catch | 0.96| 11.56|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # scikit-learn has no intervals, so statsmodels fits the negative binomial, # with spline curves for depth and temperature. curves = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), SplineTransformer(n_knots=5, include_bias=False)) gam_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("curves", curves, ["depth_m", "temperature_c"]), ("lines", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("levels", OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ]).fit(fitting[predictors]) def design(frame): return sm.add_constant(gam_recipe.transform(frame[predictors]), has_constant="add") gam_fit = sm.NegativeBinomial(fitting["abundance"].to_numpy(), design(fitting)).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=2000, disp=0) # the expected count on the log scale, and how closely it is known link = gam_fit.get_prediction(design(test), which="linear") log_low, log_high = link.conf_int(alpha=0.1).T new_catch = gam_fit.get_distribution(exog=design(test)) caught = test["abundance"].to_numpy() gam_intervals = pd.DataFrame({ "interval": ["For the average", "For a new catch"], "low": [np.exp(log_low), new_catch.ppf(0.05)], "high": [np.exp(log_high), new_catch.ppf(0.95)], }) gam_intervals["coverage"] = [np.mean((caught >= low) & (caught <= high)) for low, high in zip(gam_intervals["low"], gam_intervals["high"])] gam_intervals["width"] = [np.mean(high - low) for low, high in zip(gam_intervals["low"], gam_intervals["high"])] gam_intervals[["interval", "coverage", "width"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | interval | coverage | width | |:----------------|-----------:|--------:| | For the average | 0.25 | 5.3 | | For a new catch | 0.92 | 11.88 | ::: ::: ::: The interval for the average is 2.5 animals wide on average and holds 20% of the catches at the test sites. The interval for a new catch is 11.6 wide and holds 96% (@fig-gam-intervals), a little more than the 90% it promises, because counts are whole numbers and so are its ends. Both are right. The 399 fitting stations pin the average down closely, but single catches scatter widely around it. The interval for the average is the one a GAM draws around its curves, and the right one for a habitat description. Read as a range for the next catch, it would be wrong at 80% of the stations. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} interval_plot <- function(intervals) { intervals |> mutate(order = rank(predicted, ties.method = "first"), .by = interval) |> ggplot(aes(order)) + geom_linerange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(aes(y = caught, colour = inside), size = 1.2) + facet_wrap(~ fct_inorder(interval)) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "grey40", "FALSE" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]), labels = c("TRUE" = "Inside", "FALSE" = "Outside")) + labs(x = "Test stations, from the smallest prediction to the largest", y = "Animals caught", colour = "Catch") } interval_plot(gam_intervals) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The GAM's two 90% intervals at the test sites, ordered by the expected count. Left: the interval for the average, narrow, with most catches outside it. Right: the interval for a new catch, wide, widening as more is expected, with few catches outside. Catches outside their interval are in vermilion.](communicating-uncertainty_files/figure-html/fig-gam-intervals-1.png){#fig-gam-intervals fig-alt='Two panels, one for each interval, each showing every test station as a vertical line from its interval low end to its high end, in order of the GAM expected count from left to right, with the caught count as a point. Left, for the average: the lines are short, 2.5 animals long on average, and most points lie off them, in vermilion, above and below. Right, for a new catch: the lines are long, 11.6 animals on average, growing longer to the right, and 96% of the points lie on them, in grey.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: ### Conformal prediction gives the forest an interval The random forest is fitted to the same fitting sites. Its errors on the calibration sites set the width: each interval reaches as far either side of its prediction as the 90% point of those errors, raised slightly for the number of calibration stations. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forest <- workflow(count_recipe, rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123)) # how far 90% of the calibration errors reach, raised for their number conformal_width <- function(fitted, calibration, level = 0.9) { errors <- abs(calibration$abundance - predict(fitted, calibration)$.pred) n <- length(errors) unname(quantile(errors, min(1, ceiling((n + 1) * level) / n), type = 1)) } with_interval <- function(fitted, half_width, data) { tibble(predicted = predict(fitted, data)$.pred, low = predicted - half_width, high = predicted + half_width, caught = data$abundance, inside = caught >= low & caught <= high) } forest_fit <- fit(forest, fitting) half_width <- conformal_width(forest_fit, calibration) conformal <- with_interval(forest_fit, half_width, test) conformal |> mutate(fifth = ntile(predicted, 5)) |> summarise(coverage = mean(inside), below_zero = mean(low < 0), .by = fifth) |> arrange(fifth) |> mutate(across(-fifth, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| fifth| coverage| below_zero| |-----:|--------:|----------:| | 1| 0.98| 1.00| | 2| 0.88| 1.00| | 3| 0.98| 1.00| | 4| 0.87| 0.95| | 5| 0.79| 0.00|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} forest = pipeline(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123)) # how far 90% of the calibration errors reach, raised for their number def conformal_width(fitted, calibration, level=0.9): errors = np.abs(calibration["abundance"] - fitted.predict(calibration[predictors])) n = len(errors) return np.quantile(errors, min(1, np.ceil((n + 1) * level) / n), method="inverted_cdf") def with_interval(fitted, half_width, data): predicted = fitted.predict(data[predictors]) frame = pd.DataFrame({"predicted": predicted, "low": predicted - half_width, "high": predicted + half_width, "caught": data["abundance"].to_numpy()}) frame["inside"] = frame["caught"].between(frame["low"], frame["high"]) return frame forest_fit = forest.fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"]) half_width = conformal_width(forest_fit, calibration) conformal = with_interval(forest_fit, half_width, test) conformal["fifth"] = pd.qcut(conformal["predicted"].rank(method="first"), 5, labels=False) + 1 (conformal.assign(below_zero=conformal["low"] < 0) .groupby("fifth") .agg(coverage=("inside", "mean"), below_zero=("below_zero", "mean")) .reset_index().round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | fifth | coverage | below_zero | |--------:|-----------:|-------------:| | 1 | 1 | 1 | | 2 | 0.96 | 1 | | 3 | 0.86 | 1 | | 4 | 0.93 | 1 | | 5 | 0.73 | 0.47 | ::: ::: ::: The calibration sites set the half-width at 6.3 animals, so every interval is 12.6 wide. At the test sites it holds 90% of the catches, from a model with no distribution. Like the Normal interval of [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd), though, it has one width: it holds 98% of the catches in the fifth of stations with the smallest predictions and 79% in the fifth with the largest, and its lower end is below zero for 79% of the stations, where it is read as zero. The promise is for the stations as a whole, not for each kind of station. ### The promise holds only at stations like the calibration sites The sites a model is calibrated on are not always like the stations where it is used. Here the forest is fitted and calibrated again on the three quarters of stations with the least chlorophyll, then used on the quarter with the most. The quantile forest of [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd), whose intervals widen where its catches do, is fitted beside it on the same sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # stations without a chlorophyll reading are left out richest <- quantile(survey$chlorophyll_mg_m3, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) low_parts <- three_parts(filter(survey, chlorophyll_mg_m3 < richest)) rich <- filter(survey, chlorophyll_mg_m3 >= richest) low_forest <- fit(forest, low_parts$fitting) low_width <- conformal_width(low_forest, low_parts$calibration) quantile_fit <- workflow(count_recipe, rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123, quantreg = TRUE)) |> fit(low_parts$fitting) with_quantiles <- function(data) { ends <- predict(extract_fit_engine(quantile_fit), bake(extract_recipe(quantile_fit), new_data = data), type = "quantiles", quantiles = c(0.05, 0.95))$predictions tibble(predicted = predict(quantile_fit, data)$.pred, low = ends[, 1], high = ends[, 2], caught = data$abundance, inside = caught >= low & caught <= high) } shifted <- bind_rows( "Like the calibration sites" = bind_rows( "Forest, conformal" = with_interval(low_forest, low_width, low_parts$test), "Quantile forest" = with_quantiles(low_parts$test), .id = "interval"), "Most chlorophyll" = bind_rows( "Forest, conformal" = with_interval(low_forest, low_width, rich), "Quantile forest" = with_quantiles(rich), .id = "interval"), .id = "stations" ) shifted |> summarise(coverage = mean(inside), width = mean(high - low), average_catch = mean(caught), .by = c(stations, interval)) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|stations |interval | coverage| width| average_catch| |:--------------------------|:-----------------|--------:|-----:|-------------:| |Like the calibration sites |Forest, conformal | 0.90| 9.78| 3.04| |Like the calibration sites |Quantile forest | 0.94| 9.71| 3.04| |Most chlorophyll |Forest, conformal | 0.73| 9.78| 6.49| |Most chlorophyll |Quantile forest | 0.87| 11.58| 6.49|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # stations without a chlorophyll reading are left out richest = survey["chlorophyll_mg_m3"].quantile(0.75) low_parts = three_parts(survey[survey["chlorophyll_mg_m3"] < richest]) rich = survey[survey["chlorophyll_mg_m3"] >= richest] low_forest = forest.fit(low_parts["fitting"][predictors], low_parts["fitting"]["abundance"]) low_width = conformal_width(low_forest, low_parts["calibration"]) # scikit-learn has no quantile forest, so boosting with a quantile loss gives # the two ends, one model for each. ends = [pipeline(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", quantile=q, random_state=123)) .fit(low_parts["fitting"][predictors], low_parts["fitting"]["abundance"]) for q in (0.05, 0.95)] def with_quantiles(data): frame = pd.DataFrame({"low": ends[0].predict(data[predictors]), "high": ends[1].predict(data[predictors]), "caught": data["abundance"].to_numpy()}) frame["inside"] = frame["caught"].between(frame["low"], frame["high"]) return frame rows = [] for stations, data in [("Like the calibration sites", low_parts["test"]), ("Most chlorophyll", rich)]: for interval, frame in [ ("Forest, conformal", with_interval(low_forest, low_width, data)), ("Quantile boosting", with_quantiles(data))]: rows.append({"stations": stations, "interval": interval, "coverage": frame["inside"].mean(), "width": (frame["high"] - frame["low"]).mean(), "average_catch": frame["caught"].mean()}) pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | interval | coverage | width | average_catch | |:---------------------------|:------------------|-----------:|--------:|----------------:| | Like the calibration sites | Forest, conformal | 0.89 | 9.04 | 3.21 | | Like the calibration sites | Quantile boosting | 0.88 | 7.69 | 3.21 | | Most chlorophyll | Forest, conformal | 0.67 | 9.04 | 6.49 | | Most chlorophyll | Quantile boosting | 0.74 | 9.09 | 6.49 | ::: ::: ::: At test sites like the calibration ones, the conformal interval holds 90% of the catches. At the stations with the most chlorophyll it holds 73%, under the same label of 90% and at the same width of 9.8 animals: nothing in the interval says its promise has lapsed. The catches there average 6.5 animals against 3.0, and the errors grow with them (@fig-shift). The quantile forest's intervals are wider at these stations, 11.6 animals on average against 9.7 at the test sites like the calibration ones, and hold 87% of the catches there. Nothing promised that either. Only a check on stations like the new ones shows it, the same check that [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) makes for a prediction. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shifted |> filter(stations == "Most chlorophyll") |> interval_plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The two 90% intervals at the stations with the most chlorophyll, from models fitted and calibrated on the rest. Left: the forest's conformal interval, one width everywhere, with many large catches above it. Right: the quantile forest's, wider here than at stations like the calibration sites, with fewer catches outside. Catches outside their interval are in vermilion.](communicating-uncertainty_files/figure-html/fig-shift-1.png){#fig-shift fig-alt='Two panels, one for each interval, each showing every station in the quarter with the most chlorophyll as a vertical line from its interval low end to its high end, in order of the prediction from left to right, with the caught count as a point. Left, the forest with a conformal interval: every line is 9.8 animals long, and 27% of the points lie outside, in vermilion, most of them above the lines and towards the right. Right, the quantile forest: most lines start at zero and are of similar length, 11.6 animals on average, and the last few at the right reach higher; 87% of the points lie on them.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: ## An interval is reported with what it covers An interval helps a reader only if they can tell what it covers. Four habits make that clear: - **Name it.** "A 90% interval for a new catch", not "a 90% interval": the interval for the average is a different, narrower thing. - **Give its coverage on held-out sites** beside the level it promises. - **Say which stations set it.** Outside them, check its coverage on stations like the new ones, or say that it is unchecked. - **Give scores their interval too**, as in [Uncertainty and stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd). For one test station, from the GAM: "At 52 m and 6.6 °C on sand in winter, the model expects 3.8 animals. A new catch there would hold between 0 and 11 animals 9 times in 10, an interval that held 96% of the catches at 38 test sites." ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A **confidence interval** says where the average lies; a **prediction interval** says where one new catch may land. They answer different questions. - At new sites, the GAM's interval for the average held 20% of the catches, and its interval for a new catch 96%. A prediction interval is checked by this **coverage**. - **Conformal prediction** sets an interval for any model from its errors on **calibration** sites. The forest's held 90% at the test sites, with one width everywhere. - The promise holds only at stations like the calibration sites. At the stations with the most chlorophyll the conformal interval held 73%, at the same width and with no warning; the quantile forest's, wider at those stations, held 87%. - Report an interval with its name, its coverage on held-out sites, and the stations that set it. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Make the quantile forest conformal too. On the calibration sites, measure how far each catch falls outside its interval, as a negative number if it falls inside, and widen every interval by the conformal 90% point of those distances. How much does the width change, and the coverage at the stations with the most chlorophyll? 2. Calibrate the forest on the southern half of the survey, by `latitude`, and use it on the northern half. Does its conformal interval still hold 9 catches in 10?
